You have two kidneys. They are fist-sized organs on either side of your backbone above your waist. Your kidneys filter and clean your blood, taking out waste products and making urine. Kidney tests check to see how well your kidneys are working. They include blood, urine, and imaging tests.
Early kidney disease usually does not have signs or symptoms. Testing is the only way to know how your kidneys are doing. It is important for you to get checked for kidney disease if you have the key risk factors - diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, or a family history of kidney failure.
Specific kidney tests include:
Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) - one of the most common blood tests to check for chronic kidney disease. It tells how well your kidneys are filtering.
Creatinine blood and urine tests - check the levels of creatinine, a waste product that your kidneys remove from your blood
items.title: Kidney Tests

items.text:
Your kidneys make urine by filtering wastes and extra water from your blood. The waste is called urea. Your blood carries it to the kidneys. From the kidneys, urine travels down two thin tubes called ureters to the bladder. The bladder stores urine until you are ready to urinate. It swells into a round shape when it is full and gets smaller when empty. If your urinary system is healthy, your bladder can hold up to 16 ounces (2 cups) of urine comfortably for 2 to 5 hours.
You may have problems with urination if you have:
Kidney failure
Urinary tract infections
An enlarged prostate
Bladder control problems like incontinence, overactive bladder, or interstitial cystitis
A blockage that prevents you from emptying your bladder
Some conditions may also cause you to have blood or protein in your urine. If you have a urinary problem, see your health care provider. Urinalysis and other urine test

Foamy urine can sometimes be a sign that there is protein in your urine, a condition known as proteinuria. This happens when the kidneys are not filtering waste as effectively as they should. While foamy urine can occasionally be caused by something harmless—such as the speed of urination or residues from cleaning products in the toilet bowl—persistent foaminess over several weeks warrants a clinical evaluation.

You should schedule an appointment with a healthcare provider to investigate the cause. They will likely recommend a urinalysis, which is a simple test to check for protein, blood, or signs of infection. They may also order blood tests, such as a creatinine test or an estimation of your Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR), to determine how well your kidneys are functioning.

It is especially important to get checked if you have risk factors such as high blood pressure, diabetes, heart disease, or a family history of kidney disease, as early-stage kidney issues often do not present with obvious physical symptoms.

items.text:
A fever is a body temperature that is higher than normal. A normal temperature can vary from person to person, but it is usually around 98.6 °F (37 °C). A fever is not a disease. It is usually a sign that your body is trying to fight an illness or infection.
Infections cause most fevers. You get a fever because your body is trying to kill the virus or bacteria that caused the infection. Most of those bacteria and viruses do well when your body is at your normal temperature. But if you have a fever, it is harder for them to survive. Fever also activates your body's immune system.
Other causes of fevers include:
Medicines, including some antibiotics, blood pressure medicines, and anti-seizure medicines
Heat illness
Cancers
Autoimmune diseases
Some childhood vaccines
Treatment depends on the cause of your fever. If the fever is very high, your health care provider may recommend taking an ov

A fever that lasts for three days warrants careful attention. While many fevers resolve on their own as the body fights off an infection, you should seek immediate medical attention at the nearest hospital or by calling 112 or 199 if you experience any of the following "red flag" symptoms:

*   **Difficulty breathing or shortness of breath:** If you feel like you cannot catch your breath or are gasping for air.
*   **Altered mental state:** Confusion, extreme lethargy, difficulty waking up, or inability to stay alert.
*   **Severe headache and stiff neck:** Especially if it is accompanied by sensitivity to light or an inability to touch your chin to your chest.
*   **Persistent vomiting:** If you cannot keep any fluids down, which increases the risk of dehydration.
*   **Chest pain:** Any sharp or persistent pain in the chest area.
*   **Unexplained rash:** Particularly if the rash looks like small purple or red spots that do not fade when you press on them.
*   **Seizures:** Any uncontrolled shaking or loss of consciousness.
*   **Very high temperature:** A fever that remains persistently high (typically above 39.4°C or 103°F) and does not respond to over-the-counter fever reducers.

If you are experiencing any of these, please do not wait; go to the nearest emergency department immediately. If you are caring for someone else showing these signs and they lose consciousness, place them in the recovery position (on their side) to keep their airway clear while waiting for emergency services, and do not place anything in their mouth.

What is high blood pressure?
High blood pressure, also called hypertension, is when blood puts too much pressure against the walls of your arteries. Almost half of American adults have high blood pressure, usually with no symptoms. But it can cause serious problems such as stroke, heart failure, heart attack, and kidney disease.
What lifestyle changes can help lower high blood pressure?
Healthy lifestyle changes can help reduce high blood pressure:
Losing weight
Being physically active
Managing stress
Reducing sodium in your diet
Avoiding alcohol, tobacco, and illegal drugs
Getting enough sleep
What if lifestyle changes alone cannot lower blood pressure?
Sometimes lifestyle changes alone cannot control or lower your high blood pressure. In that case, your health care provider may prescribe blood pressure medicines.

items.text:
What is blood pressure?
Blood pressure is the force of your blood pushing against the walls of your arteries. Each time your heart beats, it pumps blood into the arteries. Your blood pressure is highest when your heart beats, pumping the blood. This is called systolic pressure. When your heart is at rest, between beats, your blood pressure falls. This is called diastolic pressure.
Your blood pressure reading uses these two numbers. Usually the systolic number comes before or above the diastolic number. For example, 120/80 means a systolic of 120 and a diastolic of 80.
How is high blood pressure diagnosed?
High blood pressure usually has no symptoms. So the only way to find out if you have it is to get regular blood pressure checks from your health care provider. Your provider will use a gauge, a stethoscope or electronic sensor, and a blood pressure cuff. They will take two or more readi

If your blood pressure readings are consistently high at home, you should schedule an appointment with a healthcare provider for a formal evaluation. A diagnosis of high blood pressure (hypertension) is typically not based on a single reading; providers often require multiple readings taken at separate times to confirm it.

During your visit, your doctor may perform physical examinations and review your medical history to determine if it is primary hypertension (which develops over time) or secondary hypertension (caused by an underlying condition or medication). 

In the meantime, consider the following steps:
*   **Keep a log:** Record the date, time, and both the systolic (top) and diastolic (bottom) numbers for every reading you take at home. This provides your doctor with helpful data.
*   **Check your technique:** Ensure you are sitting quietly for five minutes before measuring, keep your back supported, keep your feet flat on the floor, and place your arm at heart level.
*   **Lifestyle considerations:** Reducing sodium intake, increasing physical activity, managing stress, and avoiding tobacco or alcohol may support blood pressure management.

If you ever record a reading higher than 180/120 mmHg, this constitutes a potential hypertensive crisis. If you feel any symptoms like chest pain, shortness of breath, severe headache, or numbness/weakness, seek emergency medical care immediately by calling 112 or 199, or proceeding to the nearest hospital.

Most of the time, medicines make our lives better. They reduce aches and pains, fight infections, and control problems such as high blood pressure or diabetes. But medicines can also cause unwanted reactions, such as drug interactions, side effects, and allergies.
What is a drug interaction?
A drug interaction is a change in the way a drug acts in the body when taken with certain other drugs, foods, or supplements or when taken while you have certain medical conditions. Examples include:
Two drugs, such as aspirin and blood thinners
Drugs and food, such as statins and grapefruit
Drugs and supplements, such as gingko and blood thinners
Drugs and medical conditions, such as aspirin and peptic ulcers
Interactions could cause a drug to be more or less effective, cause side effects, or change the way one or both drugs work.

How can I stay safe when taking medicines?
When you start a new prescription or over-the-counter medicine, make sure you understand how to take it correctly. Know which other medicines, foods, and supplements you need to avoid. Always talk to your health care provider or pharmacist if you have questions about your medicines.

Rashes are a symptom of many different medical problems. Other causes include irritating substances and allergies. Certain genes can make people more likely to get rashes.
Contact dermatitis is a common type of rash. It causes redness, itching, and sometimes small bumps. You get the rash where you have touched an irritant, such as a chemical, or something you are allergic to, like poison ivy.
Some rashes develop right away. Others form over several days. Although most rashes clear up fairly quickly, others are long-lasting and need long-term treatment.

If you experience any difficulty breathing, swelling of the face or throat, dizziness, or a very rapid heartbeat, call 112 or 199 immediately or go to the nearest emergency room. These are signs of a severe, life-threatening reaction called anaphylaxis. 

If you are not experiencing those severe symptoms, you should take the following steps:

1. **Stop the medication:** Unless your doctor specifically told you otherwise, discontinue the use of the new medicine immediately.
2. **Contact a healthcare professional:** Call your doctor or visit a pharmacist to discuss the rash. They need to document the reaction and determine if you need an alternative medication.
3. **Seek medical assessment:** Because rashes can be caused by many different things, it is important to have a professional examine the area to distinguish between a mild side effect and a more serious condition.
4. **Avoid self-medication:** Do not apply creams, oils, or take other tablets to "clear" the rash until a doctor has assessed it, as these may mask symptoms or cause further irritation.

Keep a record of the medicine name, the date you started it, and when the rash appeared to help your doctor identify the cause.

What are cold and cough medicines?
Cold and cough medicines can help relieve symptoms of a common cold. The symptoms of a cold can include a sore throat, stuffy or runny nose, sneezing, and coughing.
You don't usually need to treat a cold or the cough that it causes. You can't cure a cold, and antibiotics won't help you get better. But sometimes the symptoms can keep you awake or cause a lot of discomfort. In that case, cold and cough medicines can sometimes be helpful.
What are the different types of cold and cough medicines?
There are lots of different cold and cough medicines, and they do different things:
Nasal decongestants - unclog a stuffy nose
Cough suppressants - quiet a cough
Expectorants - loosen mucus in your lungs so you can cough it up
Antihistamines - stop runny noses and sneezing
Pain relievers - ease fever, headaches, and minor aches and pains

What are antibiotics?
Antibiotics are medicines that fight bacterial infections in people and animals. They work by killing the bacteria or by making it hard for the bacteria to grow and multiply.
Antibiotics can be taken in different ways:
Orally (by mouth). This could be pills, capsules, or liquids.
Topically. This might be a cream, spray, or ointment that you put on your skin. It could also be eye ointment, eye drops, or ear drops.
Through an injection or intravenously (IV). This is usually for more serious infections.
What do antibiotics treat?
Antibiotics only treat certain bacterial infections, such as strep throat, urinary tract infections, and E. coli.

What is the common cold?
The common cold is a mild infection of your upper respiratory tract (which includes your nose and throat). Colds are probably the most common illness. Adults have an average of 2-3 colds per year, and children have even more. Colds are more common in the winter and spring, but you can get them at any time.
What causes the common cold?
More than 200 different viruses can cause a cold, but rhinoviruses are the most common type. The viruses that cause colds are very contagious. They can spread from person to person through the air and close personal contact. You can also get infected when you touch something that has the virus on it and then touch your eyes, mouth, or nose. For example, you could get a cold after you shake hands with someone who has a cold or touch a doorknob that has the germs on it, and then touch your face.

What is diarrhea?
Diarrhea is loose, watery stools (bowel movements). You have diarrhea if you have loose stools three or more times in one day. Acute diarrhea is diarrhea that lasts a short time. It is a common problem. It usually lasts about one or two days, but it may last longer. Then it goes away on its own.
Diarrhea lasting more than a few days may be a sign of a more serious problem. Chronic diarrhea -- diarrhea that lasts at least four weeks -- can be a symptom of a chronic disease. Chronic diarrhea symptoms may be continual, or they may come and go.
What causes diarrhea?
The most common causes of diarrhea include:
Bacteria from contaminated food or water
Viruses such as the flu, norovirus, or rotavirus . Rotavirus is the most common cause of acute diarrhea in children.

Who is at risk for diarrhea?
People of all ages can get diarrhea. On average, adults In the United States have acute diarrhea once a year. Young children have it an average of twice a year.
People who visit developing countries are at risk for traveler's diarrhea. It is caused by consuming contaminated food or water.
What other symptoms might I have with diarrhea?
Other possible symptoms of diarrhea include:
Cramps or pain in the abdomen
An urgent need to use the bathroom
Loss of bowel control
If a virus or bacteria is the cause of your diarrhea, you may also have a fever, chills, and bloody stools.

Eat smaller meals more often
Avoid strong smells, since they can sometimes trigger nausea and vomiting
If you are pregnant and have morning sickness, eat crackers before you get out of bed in the morning

cases.generated_answer:
Vomiting and diarrhea are common and often resolve on their own, typically within one or two days. However, you should seek medical attention if:

*   **Duration:** Your vomiting lasts longer than 24 hours.
*   **Dehydration:** You show signs of severe dehydration, such as extreme thirst, dry mouth, little to no urination, or dizziness when standing.
*   **Stool Characteristics:** You notice blood in your vomit or stools.
*   **Pain:** You experience severe abdominal pain.
*   **Neurological Symptoms:** You have a severe headache accompanied by a stiff neck.
*   **Poisoning:** You suspect the symptoms are a result of ingesting a toxic substance or poisoning.

If your diarrhea lasts for more than a few days, or if you are concerned about the severity of your symptoms, it is advisable to contact a healthcare provider. While waiting for a professional evaluation, prioritize staying hydrated by drinking small, frequent amounts of clear fluids.

items.text:
The urinary system is the body's drainage system for removing wastes and extra water. It includes two kidneys, two ureters, a bladder, and a urethra. Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are the second most common type of infection in the body.
You may have a UTI if you notice:
Pain or burning when you urinate
Fever, tiredness, or shakiness
An urge to urinate often
Pressure in your lower belly
Urine that smells bad or looks cloudy or reddish
Pain in your back or side below the ribs
People of any age or sex can get UTIs. But about four times as many women get UTIs as men. You're also at higher risk if you have diabetes, need a tube to drain your bladder, or have a spinal cord injury.
If you think you have a UTI it is important to see your doctor. Your doctor can tell if you have a UTI with a urine test. Treatment is with antibiotics.
NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney

items.text:
A fever is a body temperature that is higher than normal. A normal temperature can vary from person to person, but it is usually around 98.6 °F (37 °C). A fever is not a disease. It is usually a sign that your body is trying to fight an illness or infection.
Infections cause most fevers. You get a fever because your body is trying to kill the virus or bacteria that caused the infection. Most of those bacteria and viruses do well when your body is at your normal temperature. But if you have a fever, it is harder for them to survive. Fever also activates your body's immune system.
Other causes of fevers include:
Medicines, including some antibiotics, blood pressure medicines, and anti-seizure medicines
Heat illness
Cancers
Autoimmune diseases
Some childhood vaccines

Because the presence of a fever can suggest that an infection has potentially spread beyond the bladder, it is important to seek medical attention promptly. If you experience high fever, severe pain in your back or side below the ribs, shaking chills, nausea, or vomiting, you should seek medical care immediately, as these can be signs of a more serious kidney infection.

prior_observed_failures.generated_answer:
Foamy urine can sometimes indicate the presence of protein, a condition known as proteinuria. Protein in the urine is one potential sign that the kidneys may not be filtering waste products as efficiently as they should. However, foaminess can also be caused by simple factors like how quickly you urinate or the presence of cleaning agents in the toilet bowl.

Because early kidney disease often does not present with clear symptoms, you should visit a healthcare provider for an evaluation. They will likely recommend specific tests to determine the cause, including:

*   **Urinalysis:** To check for the presence of protein, blood, or signs of infection.
*   **Blood tests:** Specifically to check your creatinine levels and calculate your Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR), which measures how well your kidneys are filtering your blood.

It is particularly important to get checked if you have risk factors such as high blood pressure, diabetes, heart disease, or a family history of kidney issues. A doctor can accurately interpret these test results in the context of your overall health.

prior_observed_failures.generated_answer:
A widespread rash that develops after starting a new medicine could be a sign of an allergic reaction or a drug-related side effect. 

If you experience difficulty breathing, swelling of the face or throat, dizziness, or a very high fever, this could be a life-threatening emergency. **Immediately call 112 or 199, or go to the nearest hospital emergency department.**

If you are not experiencing those severe symptoms, take the following steps:

1. **Stop the medication:** You should pause the use of the new medicine immediately until you can consult with a healthcare professional. Do not restart it without medical advice.
2. **Contact your doctor or pharmacist:** Reach out to the person who prescribed the medicine or your local pharmacist. Explain exactly when the rash started, what the medication is, and if you have any other symptoms.
3. **Monitor the area:** Note if the rash is spreading, blistering, or becoming painful. Do not apply creams or take other medicines to treat the rash until you have spoken to a professional, as some treatments might hide symptoms or cause further irritation.

It is important to remember that rashes can have many causes, including allergies, infections, or reactions to substances that touched your skin. A doctor will need to evaluate you to determine if this is a drug reaction or something else. Be prepared to tell your doctor the name of the medicine, when you started taking it, and if you have any history of allergies.
